title: Side Effects of Bulimia: How It Affects the Body and Mind
summary: The side effects of bulimia can start early and affect the whole body. Learn the short- and long-term risks, warning signs, and what treatment can reverse.
body_markdown:
If you’re struggling with bulimia or worried about a[loved one](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/how-to-help-a-friend-with-bulimia) who is, you’re likely looking for answers, including how the condition may affect your health.[Bulimia nervosa](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/what-is-bulimia) is an eating disorder that involves episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors to “[get rid of](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/common-myths-about-bulimia) ” food and control weight. One example of a compensatory behavior is making yourself throw up.


Bulimia nervosa is a serious mental health condition that negatively affects physical and mental health. Some effects can show up almost immediately. Others occur over time. These health effects can be scary, whether you’re worried about yourself or someone you care about.


You might be wondering about the potential health effects and complications that can impact your whole body and what to do. On a hopeful note, help is available, and recovery is possible.


With treatment from a multidisciplinary care team, you can reverse many of the negative effects of bulimia nervosa. And the sooner you or a loved one engages in treatment, the better.


In this article, we explore the side effects of bulimia, what might occur in the short or long term, and more.


## **What are the side effects of bulimia?**


Bulimia nervosa can affect[nearly every bodily system](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562178/) . Bulimia health risks can seriously impact your cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, respiratory, and central nervous systems.


A common misconception is that side effects only become severe with significant weight loss. But these health issues can affect anyone, at any size.


The following table shows the wide-ranging side effects of bulimia nervosa, categorized by the areas of the body they impact.


**Side effects of bulimia by body system**


Category


Short-term effects of bulimia


Long-term effects of bulimia


How it improves with treatment


Heart and blood pressure


Low blood pressure, rapid heartbeat


Dangerous arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms), cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle); prolonged QT interval (time it takes the heart to electrically recharge between beats)


Some of these effects are caused by fluid and electrolyte imbalances; treatment may help resolve some issues; cardiac muscle damage may not be fully reversible


Fluids and electrolytes


Dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, which can trigger some heart and kidney abnormalities


Persistent dehydration and electrolyte imbalances can cause heart and kidney damage


Medical stabilization can correct the imbalances; kidney and heart function can recover, though this depends on the extent of damage


Throat and esophagus


Sore or irritated throat, acid reflux, difficulty swallowing, and hoarseness


Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and related complications; esophageal bleeding, and in rare cases even rupture


Though some throat irritation and symptoms may improve, some damage can be permanent


Stomach and intestines


Bloating, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and diarrhea


Chronic bowel dysfunction from laxative misuse; pancreatitis, gallbladder issues


Bowel dysfunction may resolve over time with proper treatment, though sometimes damage from laxative misuse may be permanent


Lungs


Aspiration of vomit into airways can cause coughing and breathing difficulties


Lung damage from aspiration; pneumothorax (collapsed lung) from forceful vomiting


Dry mouth, swollen salivary glands, dental issues, bad breath


Mouth and teeth


Dry mouth, swollen salivary glands, dental issues, bad breath


Dental enamel erosion, tooth decay, gum disease, chronic damage to salivary glands


Treatment may stop further damage, but some damage may be permanent or require extensive dental work to treat or repair


Bones and muscles


Muscle weakness or cramping


Loss of muscle mass, reduced bone mineral density, fractures; in rare cases, chronic muscle damage can also occur from electrolyte imbalances


Symptoms and issues may improve with treatment; some issues with bone may be permanent


Hormones and periods


Hormonal imbalances, irregular or missed periods, low libido


Persistent menstrual irregularities, fertility issues, risk of miscarriage


Symptoms tend to improve with treatment and recovery


Skin, eyes, hair, nails


Dry skin, brittle nails, hair loss, broken blood vessels in eyes; Russel’s sign (abrasions on knuckles from self-induced vomiting); edema (fluid retention)


The issues can persist and progress over time


Symptoms typically resolve with treatment and recovery


Mental and emotional health


Distressing feelings of guilt or shame, anxiety and depression, negative body image, trouble concentrating


Mental health issues can progress over time and increase the risk of self-harm


Evidence-based treatment helps address mental health issues over time


## **How bingeing and purging affect the body**


Many of the short- and long-term physical effects of bulimia nervosa result from the[binge-purge cycle](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/what-is-purging-disorder) that’s characteristic of the condition.


[Binge episodes](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/binge-eating-disorder) can lead to[digestive discomfort and strain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26499370/) . These episodes involve eating much more food than most people would in a discrete time period (such as two hours) and feeling a lack of control during the episode.


Purging and related compensatory behaviors to control weight after bingeing can lead to many of the short- and long-term medical complications of bulimia listed in the table above. Let’s explore these in more detail.


### Compensatory behaviors in bulimia nervosa and their side effects


Here’s how compensatory behaviors can harm your health.


**Self-induced vomiting**


Making yourself throw up can lead to a host of issues across bodily systems. It can cause[esophageal (“food pipe”) damage](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9258367/) , for example. It can also cause gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and complications from it, including[Barrett’s esophagus](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9258367/) .


Forcing yourself to vomit can lead to significant[dental damage](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10573129/) to gums and teeth or[salivary gland enlargement](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5878158/) . It can also cause “[Russel’s sign](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/14782715241228325) ,” abrasions on your knuckles from scraping them on your teeth.


Your eyes can also incur damage from[pressure](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4803618/) related to forceful vomiting, leading to broken blood vessels and bleeding.


Self-induced vomiting can also affect the lungs via[aspiration](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4392812/) , which is when you accidentally inhale stomach contents into your airways.


One of the most concerning side effects of throwing up on purpose is electrolyte imbalance.[Electrolyte imbalance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36346630/) can cause low blood pressure, kidney issues, and[cardiovascular disease or heart damage](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40345991/) . These issues can ultimately be fatal.

**Laxative misuse**


[Misusing laxatives](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/laxative-abuse) can lead to short- and long-term digestive system dysfunction, including issues with diarrhea or constipation. In some cases,[bowel perforation](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537224/) (when intestinal contents leak into your abdominal cavity) or other types of damage can occur. As with self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse can also lead to electrolyte imbalances that harm cardiovascular and kidney health.


**Diuretic misuse**


Diuretics encourage your kidneys to flush fluids out of your body in your urine.[Diuretic misuse](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eat.20814) can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalances rather quickly, leading to organ damage if not corrected.


**Fasting and food restriction**


Fasting and food restriction can drive[malnutrition](https://www.who.int/health-topics/malnutrition#tab=tab_1) . Malnutrition can lead to low energy, weakened muscles or[loss of muscle mass](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40597420/) , and decreased bone mineral density, which increases your risk of[fractures](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5675561/) .


Malnutrition can affect skin and hair health. It can cause[edema](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562178/) (fluid buildup and swelling). And it can lead to dry skin, hair loss, and brittle nails.


Malnutrition also affects[cognitive function](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42747849/) , potentially leading to issues concentrating or thinking clearly.


Additionally, fasting and food restriction can lead to hormonal disturbances that can disrupt your menstrual cycle. Up to 64% of menstruating people with bulimia have oligomenorrhea (infrequent periods). And up to 40% have[amenorrhea](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/amenorrhea-and-eating-disorders) (the absence of a period), according to 2020 research in the[Journal of Eating Disorders](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12771763/) . These issues also have a direct impact on fertility and can lead to[miscarriage](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5134748/) if you become pregnant.


**Compulsive exercise**


Overexercising can cause[injuries](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5386595/) . It can also worsen or lead to electrolyte imbalances or[relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S)](https://equip.health/articles/food-and-fitness/red-s-syndrome-relative-energy-deficiency-in-sport) , in which you burn more calories than you take in. Compulsive exercise can also drive the same[menstrual cycle impacts](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32139174/) and skin and hair changes as fasting and food restriction.


If you’re recognizing any of the following compensatory behaviors in yourself or a loved one and are unsure if it’s bulimia,[Equip’s free eating disorder screener](https://equip.health/is-it-an-eating-disorder) can help you determine risk level and next steps.


## **How serious are the side effects of bulimia?**


The side effects of bulimia are very serious, as some can lead to dangerous issues with your heart, kidneys, and other organs.


### **How soon can side effects start?**


Some side effects can take a while to progress. But electrolyte disturbances can show up[within hours](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1354750X.2024.2361074) or a couple of days in some cases.[Electrolytes](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541123/) help manage the electrical activity throughout your body, including your heart. That’s one reason why imbalances are so dangerous.


“With rapid electrolyte shifts, this directly affects the cardiovascular system,” says Nikki Kirby, RD, at Equip. “This causes an abnormal rhythm and can lead to sudden cardiac arrest or death. This can show up very quickly since a patient does not know whether their electrolytes are in a safe range or not.”

### **Can bulimia be fatal?**


Yes, bulimia can lead to death. People with bulimia nervosa are nearly twice as likely to die when compared to people in the general population, according to research published in the journal[Current Opinion in Psychiatry](https://www.ovid.com/jnls/co-psychiatry/fulltext/10.1097/yco.0000000000000739~incidence-prevalence-and-mortality-of-anorexia-nervosa-and) . Deaths can occur from physical complications or from[suicide.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40048192/)


The statistics are understandably frightening. The important thing to know is that the side effects of bulimia are indeed serious, but help is available. Don’t hesitate to seek help from a multidisciplinary care team if you’re concerned about any disordered eating behaviors or symptoms you’re experiencing.


“The earlier a patient can get treatment, the better,” Kirby says.


### **Symptoms that need urgent medical care**


Some symptoms require immediate medical attention, such as going to the emergency room, according to Kirby.


**Seek help right away for yourself or a loved one if you or they experience:**


- Blood in vomit, stool, or urine
- Vomit that looks like coffee grounds
- Stool that looks black or tarry
- Urine that is brown, red, or tea-colored
- Dizziness
- Fainting
- Rapid heartbeat or heart palpitations
- Low blood pressure
- Going 24 hours without fluids or food


## **What are the psychological effects of bulimia?**


Bulimia nervosa also takes a toll on your[mental health](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/eating-disorders-and-anxiety) . Feelings of[shame or guilt](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30182527/) can crop up with the binge-purge cycle, for example. And more than 76% of people with bulimia also have depression, according to 2025 research published in[JAMA](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40048192/) .


“Eating disorders are a mental illness *with* physical symptoms,” Kirby says, “which means there are many psychological and social impacts alongside the physical damage from the diagnosis.”


She adds, “I will often have a patient reflect on their life and eating prior to the onset of the eating disorder. I will then compare it to their current struggles:[fear of eating around others](https://equip.health/articles/food-and-fitness/fear-of-eating-in-front-of-others) , guilt associated with certain types of food, social withdrawal, and dominating food-related thoughts. Oftentimes, patients do not realize how much life and joy the eating disorder has taken away from them. And these can be great motivators to fight for recovery.”


## **Can the side effects of bulimia be reversed?**


Whether the side effects of bulimia can be reversed depends on many factors and varies widely from person to person. Some side effects of bulimia may resolve with[treatment](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/bulimia-treatment) , while others could have lasting damage.


“Patients often ask if it is possible to reverse symptoms,” Kirby says. “Reassuring them that other patients have achieved symptom improvement and full recovery can be encouraging.”


She adds, “I like to treat the entire process as an ‘experiment.’ Patients have engaged in the same behaviors for a long time, causing damage. Now, we can try something different with nourishment and eliminating behaviors and see what improvements they feel. They might notice their hair stopped falling out, more mental clarity, increased energy, all the way up to improved blood pressure, electrolytes, and digestion.”

## **How to get help for bulimia**


Bulimia nervosa is best treated with the support of a multidisciplinary care team, such as the type you’ll find at Equip.


Therapeutic approaches, including[enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E)](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/CBT-e-enhanced-cognitive-behavioral-therapy-for-eating-disorders) , under the guidance of an eating disorder-informed therapist, to help to address the mental health component of bulimia nervosa.


Additionally, working with a registered dietitian supports re-nourishment and helps establish normal eating habits. And working with a medical professional helps correct electrolyte imbalances and other health concerns.


Reach out for a[consultation](https://my.equip.health/) and to get started. You don’t have to wait for things to get worse before they get better.


## **The bottom line**


Bulimia nervosa can affect nearly every system in the body, including brain health. Some of the negative side effects stem from compensatory behaviors, such as self-induced vomiting or laxative misuse. Others occur from food restriction or compulsive exercise.


The negative health effects can become serious rather quickly, as electrolyte imbalances can damage the heart or other organs if they aren’t addressed. These factors make bulimia nervosa a scary condition, whether you’re worried about yourself or a loved one.


Help is available, and treatment and recovery can reverse many of the negative physical and mental health concerns that bulimia nervosa brings on. Improved health and well-being are within reach.


## **FAQ**


### Why does bulimia cause swollen cheeks?


A characteristic of bulimia nervosa is using compensatory behaviors to “get rid” of food. Self-induced vomiting is an example. This can cause a condition called bilateral parotid sialadenosis, an enlargement of your salivary glands. This is why bulimia can sometimes cause swollen cheeks.


### Is bulimia a mental illness?


Yes, bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder and mental illness. It is listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5).


### Does bulimia damage your throat permanently?


The self-induced vomiting that is a common part of bulimia nervosa can damage your throat. Whether the damage is permanent or reversible varies. In some cases, damage can heal with treatment and recovery. However, some damage may persist long term or indefinitely.
